claims.text: Premelting and melting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by inherent chemical heterogeneities.
Chemical heterogeneities create nanoscale regions with locally reduced melting points.
Locally reduced melting points broaden the phase transition and cause it to progress gradually relative to homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are solid and single-phase.
The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are chemically homogeneous.
The proposed test uses a linear temperature ramp under an inert atmosphere with in situ monitoring.
Single-metal or simple binary baseline nanoparticles exhibit sharp melting transitions.
Local short-range-order variations or elemental segregation produce spatial variations in bonding energies.
Chemical heterogeneities generate local regions with lower cohesive energy.
Regions with lower cohesive energy cause premature surface disordering and staggered melting onset.
Different nanoparticle regions reach their local melting points at different temperatures, producing a broadened melting transition.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will begin localized disordering earlier than homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
Localized disordering will often initiate at the nanoparticle surface.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will melt over a broader temperature range than homogeneous baseline nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies to 5–50 nm nanoparticles under quasi-equilibrium heating in inert environments.
Non-equilibrium conditions or significant morphological variation may alter the predicted behavior.
Failure to observe either earlier localized premelting or a statistically broader melting transition relative to the matched baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial particles are described as chemically homogeneous, while the hypothesis simultaneously treats inherent chemical heterogeneities, including elemental segregation, as the governing initial structural feature. This could be reconciled by distinguishing macroscale compositional uniformity from nanoscale fluctuations, but that distinction is not stated.
